ImageDescription.value:
Description: Early Anglo-Saxon pyramidal mount made from silver and inlaid with niello, in the shape of a truncated four-sided hollow pyramid with a strap bar on the underside. On each of the four sides and on the apex there is geometric decoration of engraved lines inlaid with niello. On the top is a square with a short line leading inwards about a third of the way down opposing faces, forming a square S shape in the silver. Those on the sides comprise two pairs of designs on opposing faces. Each face is outlined with a nielloed border; one design also has a central vertical line cutting through two horizontal stepped lines forming a battlement pattern. The other design has an inverted T at the base, with a vertical line connecting the centre of the upright stem to the centre of the upper horizontal border line, and two oblique lines connecting the upper corners of the cross-piece of the T to the middle of the oblique border lines. Some of the niello is decomposed and some missing; there are occasional spots of iron corrosion.

An integral silver bar runs across the centre of the hollowed reverse; this is 2.5mm wide and flat in cross-section at either end, but thinner and narrower (1mm wide) towards the centre. The bar is slightly concave on the sides and reverse face, at least some of the concavity being due to wear.

Dimensions: 12.3 x 12.3 at base, 5.5mm in height. Weight 2.01g.

Discussion: The function of pyramidal mounts is still uncertain, but it seems likely that they were used to help secure the sword in the scabbard. Two were famously found in the high-status graves of Sutton Hoo Mound 1, but they are relatively uncommon grave finds. They are however common accidental losses, with 54 on the PAS database to date including this find (6 in gold, 20 in silver and 28 in copper alloy). See SUR-E6B3B4 for an example of a silver pyramid with a similarly narrowed bar.

This example is not quite like any other pyramid known, although many examples carry niello inlay. The stepped or zig-zag pattern is found on other artefact types, notably buckle plates and belt mounts, and is arguably an imitation of a cloisonné cellwork pattern (Adams 2011, 25-27). See BERK-1DF3D2 for another example of a silver sword pyramid with stepped or zig-zag faux cloisonné niello lines).

Date: Pyramidal mounts of this type were introduced in the early seventh century and continued in use for the rest of the century. During the course of the seventh century the pyramids become taller and their bases take on more various shapes, becoming circular, hexagonal and octagonal as well as square. The relatively low shape and small size of this example indicates a date in the first half of the century.

ImageDescription.value:
A nearly complete cast copper alloy mount, probably dating to the Medieval period. The mount is square in plan and pyramidal in cross-section, with a hollow reverse surface and an integrally cast square-sectioned shaft. A small portion of the mount shaft has broken off; there is a small fragment of attached copper alloy on the upper portion of the shaft, that seems to be casting waste. The outer surface of the mount has a flat border, before rising into a pyramid from the centre. It measures 30.66 in length and width, 17.71 mm thick and weighs 15.56 grams.

Pyramidal mounts with integral shafts were used during the Medieval period for decoration on belts, harness straps and caskets or furniture. The relative size and weight of this example suggests perhaps that this was used for horse harness straps or caskets, rather than an item of personal adornment.

Similar mounts are common in the Early Medieval period; however, Early Medieval mounts commonly have a horizontal strap bar on the reverse surface instead of a mount shaft as this example has. Early Medieval pyramidal mounts may have adorned belts, scabbards, sword harnesses, etc (cf. MacGregor and Bolick, 1993, 'Summary Catalogue of the Anglo-Saxon Collections', BAR 230, p.210). For some PAS database examples of Early Medieval mounts, cf. WILT-9AB1A4; BH-31B1B5.

The Art Deco Gulf Tower in Pittsburgh.

We begin our slideshow of Pittsburgh with architecture. This is the top of the Gulf Tower which was built by Gulf Oil (long before it became part of Chevron).

Wikipedia has this to say: [The Gulf Tower was] designed by the firm of Trowbridge & Livingston and completed in 1932 at a cost of $10.05 million ($140.4 million today). Now called Gulf Tower, it has 44 floors and rises 177.4 m (582 ft) above Downtown Pittsburgh. The crown of the skyscraper is modeled after the Mausoleum of Halicarnassus in the style of a step pyramid. The building was listed as a Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation Historic Landmark in 1973.

132449427.title: File:Pyramid of the Estate Society (Catalá annotations).jpg

ImageDescription.value:
Today many countries enjoy more freedom than ever before, but progress has always been slow and difficult and has been achieved thanks to thousands and thousands of unsung heroes.

Not many centuries ago, the system of government in Europe was absolutism, a system that began in the Middle Ages and in which society was segmented into social strata, with a King located at the top of the pyramid and below it. all the population separated by estates.

The First Estate. It was the Church that as an Institution owned large tracts of land and had the privilege of not paying taxes. The most important clerics They came from the nobility. Most religious knew how to read and write and had some kind of education.

The Second Estate. It was formed by the Nobility and by the high military commanders who also used to be nobles. Like the Church, they owned large tracts of land and enjoyed the privilege of not paying taxes. Most did not work and lived off the income provided by the peasants who worked their land.

The Third Estate or Third Estate. It was made up of the rest of the population, which was the most numerous and the poorest. The majority were illiterate peasants who, since they did not own land, earned their living working those of the Church or those of the Nobles. The Most were not wage earners but paid rent to the owner and kept a part of the harvest. They had to pay taxes to the state. In the cities lived merchants and artisans who depended on the King to whom they paid taxes.

It should be remembered that during the 16th and 17th centuries, more than 80% of the population lived in the countryside and worked in agriculture. Over time the percentage slowly decreased, but that tremendously unfair type of society was maintained for a long time because those at the top of the pyramid used all means to ensure that nothing changed (the Extractive Elites abhor change).

Artist.value: Pablo Carlos Budassi

132449428.title: File:Pyramid of the Estate Society (no annotations).jpg

ImageDescription.value:
A día de hoy muchos países gozan de más libertad que antes, pero los progresos siempre han sido lentos y difíciles y se han conseguido gracias a miles y miles de héroes anónimos.

No hace muchos siglos que que el sistema de gobierno de Europa era el Absolutismo, un sistema que empezó en la Edad Media y en el que la sociedad estaba segmentada en estratos sociales, con un Rey situado en la cúspide de la pirámide y debajo de él toda la población separada por estamentos.

El Primer Estamento. Era la Iglesia que como Institución poseía grandes extensiones de tierra y tenia el privilegio de no pagar impuestos. Los clérigos con cargos más importantes procedían de la nobleza. La mayoría de religiosos sabia leer y escribir y tenían algún tipo de educación.

El Segundo Estamento. Estaba formado por la Nobleza y por los altos mandos militares que también solían ser nobles. Al igual que la Iglesia poseían grandes extensiones de tierra y gozaban del privilegio de no pagar impuestos. La mayoría no trabajaba y vivía de las rentas que les proporcionaban los campesinos que trabajaban sus tierras.

El Tercer Estamento o Tercer Estado. Lo formaba el resto de población que era la más numerosa y la más pobre. La mayoría eran campesinos analfabetos que como no tenían tierras en propiedad se ganaban la vida trabajando las de la Iglesia o las de los Nobles. La mayoría no eran asalariados sino que pagaban una renta al señor propietario y se quedaban con una parte de la cosecha. Tenían de pagar impuestos al estado. En las ciudades vivían mercaderes y artesanos que dependían del Rey al que le pagaba impuestos.

Cabe recordar que durante los siglos XVI y XVII más de un 80% de la población vivía en el campo y trabajaba en la agricultura. Con el tiempo el porcentaje fue disminuyendo lentamente, pero aquel tipo de sociedad tremendamente injusta se mantuvo durante mucho tiempo porque los de arriba de la pirámide se valían de todos los medios para que nada cambiase (las Elites Extractivas aborrecen los cambios).

ImageDescription.value:
A silver gilt Anglo-Saxon pyramidal mount (sword pyramid), probably a fitting from a scabbard dating from the early seventh century. The mount is hollow and each of the four triangular panels is decorated with an inverted U-shape with the ends of the arms curling back on themselves. Each U-shape has a central groove running along its length. The pyramid is truncated and the top is set with a small square of garnet. The sides of the mount retain traces of gilding. A portion of the rim on three sides has chipped away. It is 16.3mm long, 16.3mm wide and 10.3mm high. It weighs 2.86gm.On the reverse is a stub of an oval-sectioned bar which looks as if it would have crossed the base of the mount allowing a strap to be tucked behind it.

Sword pyramids are small fittings used in connection with the straps on sword scabbard. They are now common finds from Anglo-Saxon England. They were apparently very prone to loss. They are also widespread on the continent, usually made from silver or copper alloy (Menghin 1983; map 22).

Similar objects on the database are: LIN-05D862 and WAW-7A89A7, both with the inverted U-shape decoration on the side panels; also HAMP-2C1D52, BUC-90E4A7, BERK-1DF3D2, NLM401, and SF1479. Another relief-decorated pyramid with a garnet on the apex can be found at NMS-EEF020. Similar scabbard fittings can also be seen in the Treasure Annual Report 2007, p98 - 99 , Fig: 166, 169 and 171 (Treasure cases 2007 T25, 2007 T188 and 2007 T477). Compare also to TAR 2002, number 67 and TAR 2003 number 116.

This shape of pyramid, with a relatively low apex, can be dated to the first half of the seventh century.

ImageDescription.value:
An incomplete gilt-silver pyramidal sword scabbard mount of early-medieval (Anglo-Saxon) date.

Description: The pyramid mount is decorated on all four sides with incised double Y-shaped lines forming three triangular panels. Within each panel is a recessed triangular impression, the lower two point up and the upper one of each point down. On the peak of the mount is a square cell that would have likely held a garnet or other decorative insert, now missing. The underside of the mount is hollow, the original strap bar across the base for attachment is now missing surviving only as vestigial scars on each side. The silver is heavily oxidised leaving the mount a dull grey colour, the gilding is also heavily worn.

Measurements: 12.42mm x 12.18mm x 7.98mm and 3.3g in weight.

Discussion: Pyramidal mounts such as this one appear to have been used on scabbards, perhaps to secure the sword in the scabbard or to attach the scabbard to the sword belt. There are many now recorded on the PAS database and approximately 40% are made of silver. The main period of use appears to be the last years of the sixth century and first half of the seventh century, with the low square pyramidal shape most popular at this time. The mounts increase in variety, height and rarity later in the seventh century. A parallel, albeit in copper alloy, has been recorded from Crowmarsh, Oxfordshire (<a href="https://finds.org.uk/database/artefacts/record/id/765065">BH-B72FCB</a>) while a direct parallel in silver has been recorded from Bygrave, Hertfordshire (2007 T25, <a href="https://finds.org.uk/database/artefacts/record/id/245669">BH-460DE6</a>). Excavated examples remain relatively rare although a pair were recovered from Grave 174 at the Meads Cemetary, Sittingbourne, Kent, treasure case 2008T550.

Conclusion: It is therefore clear that this object likely dates to before 1719 and as the object is made of more than 10% precious metals, it constitutes potential Treasure under the stipulations of The Treasure Act 1996.
